notes: Ruling slot 22 = Biafran Armed Forces under Ojukwu (head of state, no party since all were banned in 1966); coalition slot 13 = the civilian Executive Council around Philip Effiong. English is the language of Biafran public life, so catchy factions use English labels except Igbo terms. Islamic slots use the small Lebanese Shia trading community and Igbo/Nigerian Muslim milieus.

0.name: The Libreville Connection
0.text:
The Libreville Connection is the web of envoys, airlift organisers and arms buyers who tie Biafra to its last foreign patrons: Gabon's Omar Bongo, Côte d'Ivoire's Félix Houphouët-Boigny and, behind them, Jacques Foccart's African cell in Paris. On 1 January 1970 its night flights into Uli are the only line keeping the enclave supplied as the federal offensive closes in.

Its members want Biafra to survive as a Western-backed client state, anti-communist and friendly to France, buying recognition with oil concessions. Its leverage lies in the relief and arms flights, in foreign bank accounts, and in the exit routes it can open for the leadership when the front collapses.

1.name: Ibo State Union
1.text:
The Ibo State Union is the pan-Igbo cultural and welfare federation built from the town and clan improvement unions of the 1940s. Banned with all political associations by the federal military government in May 1966, its networks of elders, teachers and town-union officers carried the mass mobilisation of 1967 and still run much of local life inside the shrinking enclave.

It stands for communal self-help, Christian respectability, education and the protection of Igbo property and people. Conservative and pro-Western in outlook, it sees Britain as a betrayer but still looks to the West for rescue. Its strength lies in the town unions, which collect money and men in every village.

2.name: Consultative Assembly
2.text:
The Consultative Assembly is the body of delegates from every province of the former Eastern Region that, together with the Advisory Committee of Chiefs and Elders, mandated Ojukwu to proclaim the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967. It meets rarely now, but remains the only representative forum the republic has, giving civilian notables a claim to share in decisions.

Its members favour constitutional government, elected institutions after the war and a negotiated settlement rather than fighting to the last village. Lawyers, civil servants and professionals fill its ranks, and its leverage lies in the legitimacy it can lend to, or withhold from, any surrender or peace terms.

3.name: National Council of Nigerian Citizens
3.text:
The National Council of Nigerian Citizens is the nationalist party of Nnamdi Azikiwe that governed the Eastern Region until the military coup of January 1966 and was then dissolved with all parties. Its regional machine under former premier Michael Okpara became the political backbone of secession, but Azikiwe himself returned to the federal side in 1969 and now urges reunification.

The party stands for welfare-state development, mass education, free enterprise tempered by public planning and a federal Nigeria in which the East keeps its weight. Its leverage lies in old ward organisations, in Okpara's standing as adviser to Ojukwu and in Azikiwe's prestige as a possible broker of peace.

4.name: The Nsukka Marxists
4.text:
The Nsukka Marxists are lecturers, teachers and students of the evacuated University of Nigeria who read Lenin and Fanon in refugee camps and directorate offices. Few in number and without an organisation of their own, they gather around the radical publicists of the war effort and argue that the struggle can only be won as a social revolution.

They want land, banks and trade taken into public ownership and the old merchant and chiefly elite swept aside. Their great problem is Moscow, whose MiGs and Ilyushins fly for Lagos, so they seek sympathy in the wider communist movement rather than patronage. Their leverage lies in the classrooms and propaganda offices where they work.

5.name: Biafran Organization of Freedom Fighters
5.text:
The Biafran Organization of Freedom Fighters is the guerrilla arm raised in 1968–69 to fight behind federal lines, ambushing convoys, cutting roads and organising villages under occupation. Recruited from students, schoolboys, demobilised soldiers and local volunteers, it operates in small bands and answers only loosely to the military directorates.

Its cadres have absorbed the Ahiara Declaration's call for a people's revolution and see the war as a struggle against neo-colonialism, not only against Lagos. They favour arming the peasantry, punishing profiteers and fighting on in the bush whatever happens to the regular army. Their leverage lies in their weapons and their claim to be the last fighters if the front breaks.

6.name: Directorate of Propaganda
6.text:
The Directorate of Propaganda is the information machine of the republic, run by Uche Chukwumerije and supplied by Radio Biafra, the Biafra Newsletter and an overseas press service in Geneva. Its broadcasts have kept a starving population mobilised for two and a half years, branding the war a genocide backed by Britain and the Soviet Union.

Its writers champion a hard, anti-imperialist Biafran nationalism, hostile to London, Moscow and Washington alike and contemptuous of any talk of compromise. They demand discipline, sacrifice and purity at home. Their leverage lies in the radio transmitters and the presses, the only voices most Biafrans still hear.

7.name: Biafran Militia
7.text:
The Biafran Militia is the mass auxiliary force raised in 1967 to guard roads, bridges and villages and to feed recruits into the army. Organised by province and division, it reaches every community still under Biafran control and works with the military police and civil defence committees in hunting saboteurs.

Its commanders believe in total mobilisation under one leadership: conscription, requisition, curfews and harsh punishment of defeatists, with no room for parties or civilian bickering. Hostile to Britain and the Soviet Union for arming Nigeria, they prize obedience above all. Their leverage lies in their presence at every checkpoint and in the fear their tribunals inspire.

8.name: The Levantine Traders
8.text:
The Levantine Traders are the Lebanese and Syrian merchant families who ran cloth, transport and produce businesses in Onitsha, Aba, Port Harcourt and Enugu before the war. Most are Shia from south Lebanon; many fled in 1967, but a few stayed on with Biafran passes, trading through the blockade and keeping links to Beirut.

Their religious life follows the moderate reformism preached by Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose new Supreme Islamic Shia Council courts emigrants across West Africa. Politically they seek protection, contracts and neutrality, avoiding open loyalty to Lagos or to the secessionists. Their leverage lies in capital, foreign currency and smuggling routes that every side needs.

9.name: The Port Harcourt Husayniyya
9.text:
The Port Harcourt Husayniyya is a small congregation of Lebanese Shia shopkeepers and their sons who gather for Muharram mourning and religious instruction in the port city, under federal control since May 1968. Its members correspond with seminarians in Najaf and listen to clerics who reject the accommodating line of the Lebanese notables.

They hold that political authority belongs to the learned jurists and regard the Westernised trading families as morally compromised. Their influence on the war is minute; they care more for faith and family than for flags. Their leverage lies only in remittances and their ties to the clerical circles of Najaf and Jabal Amil.

10.name: Ndi Alakuba
10.text:
Ndi Alakuba are the Igbo converts to Islam, concentrated around Enugu-Ezike in the Nsukka highlands and among traders who learned the faith in the North. A small community even before 1966, it was overrun early in the war, and its members now live under federal administration or as refugees inside the enclave.

Led by local imams and elders, it is quietist, loyal to whatever authority holds the land and anxious to show that Islam is not the enemy's religion. It favours peace, the return of property and protection by the established Islamic bodies of Nigeria. Its leverage lies in being a bridge between Igbo communities and the Muslim North.

11.name: The Al-Azhar Circle
11.text:
The Al-Azhar Circle is a handful of Nigerian students and teachers returned from Cairo and Medina who preach in the market mosques of the eastern towns. Marginal before the war and scattered by it, they now live mostly under federal control, where they denounce both the secessionists and the federal soldiers as men without religion.

They argue that only a restored caliphate governed by the sharia can end Africa's wars of tribes and states, and look back to the Sokoto jihad of Usman dan Fodio as their model. They reject Christian-led nationalism outright. Their leverage is negligible beyond a few study circles and the prestige of Arabic learning.

12.name: Muslim Students' Society of Nigeria
12.text:
The Muslim Students' Society of Nigeria is the federation of Muslim pupils and undergraduates founded in Lagos in 1954 to defend Islamic education in a school system dominated by Christian missions. Its few eastern branches were broken up when the war began, but its graduates are rising in Lagos, Ibadan and Zaria.

It stands for modern Islamic education, moral reform and Muslim participation in public life within a united Nigeria, close in spirit to reformist movements in Egypt and Sudan. Toward the enclave it is a voice for reconciliation and relief. Its leverage lies in an educated membership that will staff the professions and the civil service.

13.name: Executive Council
13.text:
The Executive Council is the cabinet of civilian commissioners and senior officers through which Ojukwu governs the republic, backed by a civil service evacuated from Enugu to Umuahia and now to Owerri. Chief of General Staff Philip Effiong is its leading soldier, and its administrators run food directorates, refugee camps and the Biafran pound.

Its members are pragmatists: they keep the state working, ration scarce supplies and increasingly ask how a surrender could be managed without massacre. They are neither Western clients nor revolutionaries, but loyal to orderly administration. Their leverage lies in the machinery of government, which any successor, Biafran or federal, will need.

14.name: Advisory Committee of Chiefs and Elders
14.english: Advisory Committee of Chiefs and Elders
14.text:
The Advisory Committee of Chiefs and Elders gathers the traditional rulers, title-holders and senior men of the Igbo, Ibibio, Efik and Ijaw communities who sat with the Consultative Assembly in May 1967. It voted for secession and still lends the regime the authority of age and custom, though the minority-area chiefs are now mostly under federal rule.

Its members defend land tenure, customary courts, the dignity of chieftaincy and the authority of elders over the young men in uniform. They prefer an end to the war that protects homes and farms to a fight to the death. Their leverage lies in village loyalties and in being the channel through which surrender would be negotiated.

15.name: Bank of Biafra
15.text:
The Bank of Biafra is the central bank that issued the Biafran pound in 1968 and manages the republic's dwindling foreign reserves under its governor Sylvester Ugoh. Around it gather the bankers, contractors and import agents who handle arms purchases, relief funds and the hard currency kept in European accounts.

They stand for sound money, private trade and the protection of property, and they quietly fear that the end of the war will make the Biafran pound worthless overnight. Pragmatic rather than ideological, they keep channels open to Lagos and London. Their leverage lies in their control of whatever money Biafra still has.

16.name: Ahia Attack
16.text:
Ahia Attack, the attack trade, is the name Biafrans give to the traders, mostly women, who slip across the front lines to buy salt, fish, cloth and medicine in federal-held markets and sell them inside the enclave. Tolerated, taxed and sometimes punished by the authorities, they keep entire districts alive in the final winter of the war.

They want free movement of goods, an end to requisitions and price controls, and no state standing between a trader and her market. Indifferent to grand ideology, they distrust the directorates and federal soldiers alike. Their leverage lies in supplying food that neither army can provide.

17.name: Biafran Land Army
17.text:
The Land Army is the food-production campaign launched to turn schools, refugees and idle land into farms as the blockade starved the enclave. Agricultural officers, mission workers and the food directorates organise communal plots of cassava, yam and vegetables, and promote fishing and the use of every available patch of soil.

Its organisers preach self-reliance, careful use of land and water, and village production instead of imported food, ideas drawn from mission agriculture and the Ahiara Declaration. They distrust large plantations and oil installations alike. Their leverage lies in feeding refugees when the relief flights fail.

18.name: National Guidance Committee
18.text:
The National Guidance Committee is the body of intellectuals, including the novelist Chinua Achebe, that drafted the Ahiara Declaration, proclaimed by Ojukwu on 1 June 1969 as the principles of the Biafran Revolution. Its writers, academics and civil servants run political education for officers, students and civil defence committees across the enclave.

They call for a just and egalitarian society, public control of key resources, an end to profiteering and a leadership accountable to the people, free of both Western and Soviet tutelage. Their programme speaks to students, teachers and junior officers. Their leverage lies in the ideological authority of the Declaration itself.

19.name: The Peking Line
19.text:
The Peking Line is a small group of students, teachers and young officers who took heart when the People's Republic of China declared its sympathy for Biafra in 1968. Reading Mao's writings on protracted war, they argue that the enclave must abandon conventional fronts and turn itself into a liberated peasant base.

They denounce the Soviet Union as an imperialist power arming Lagos and look to China as the only great power on the side of oppressed peoples. They want rural communes, people's militias and a break with the merchant elite. Their leverage is modest: pamphlets, a few guerrilla commanders and the despair of a war conventional armies are losing.

20.name: Biafra Kwenu
20.text:
Biafra Kwenu, named after the rallying cry shouted at every gathering, is the mass nationalism of returning refugees, market women, veterans and youth who lived through the pogroms of 1966. It has no single organisation, but its voice fills rallies, church halls and the songs of the front.

It holds that Easterners can never again be safe inside Nigeria, rejects any return to federal rule and distrusts educated leaders it suspects of preparing a deal. It is fiercely populist and suspicious of foreigners and of the minority peoples who sided with Lagos. Its leverage lies in sheer numbers and in the anger any leader who surrenders must face.

21.name: The Owerri Die-Hards
21.text:
The Owerri Die-Hards are the officers and commanders who recaptured Owerri in April 1969 and believe the war can still be prolonged, whatever the cost in lives. Grouped around front-line brigades and military tribunals, they treat every peace feeler as treason and every refugee as a potential recruit.

They want total war: conscription of every male, summary justice for saboteurs and resistance to the last village even if Uli falls. Their nationalism has hardened into a cult of sacrifice, distrustful of civilians, churches and foreign mediators alike. Their leverage lies in the guns of the last organised units and in their power to block any capitulation.

22.name: Biafran Armed Forces
22.text:
The Biafran Armed Forces, the army, small air force and navy of the Republic of Biafra, have governed the secessionist state since May 1967 under Head of State General Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu. After thirty months of war they hold only a shrinking enclave around Owerri, Orlu and the Uli airstrip, short of food, fuel and ammunition as the federal Third Marine Commando drives north.

The officer corps fuses Biafran nationalism with military command: power rests with Ojukwu and his Chief of General Staff, Philip Effiong, while civilian bodies merely advise. Its leverage is total but fragile, resting on the soldiers' loyalty, the Uli airlift and the people's fear of what defeat will bring.

23.name: Ndi Eze
23.text:
Ndi Eze, the kings, are the traditional monarchs of the East: the Obi of Onitsha, the Eze Nri, the Obong of Calabar and the many town kings recognised by the old Eastern Regional government. Their palaces are occupied or in ruins, and most now reign over refugees, yet their titles keep a sacred authority untouched by the war.

They stand for the continuity of royal institutions, customary law and the ritual order of land and lineage, whatever flag flies over the region. Pragmatists, they will make terms with the victor to save their towns. Their leverage lies in their role as guardians of community and as natural intermediaries for peace.
